newsitem.title: USA: U.S. criteria wide in Conrail merger review.
newsitem.headline: U.S. criteria wide in Conrail merger review.

text.p: An official of the Surface Transportation Board said on Tuesday that issues the board weighs when judging rail mergers, such as that of Conrail Inc., range from adequacy of rail service to price paid.
In addition, David Konschnik, director of the board's office of proceedings, said the board also can order a sell-off of parallel tracks to ease any anticompetitive effects.

Konschnik told the House of Representatives Transportation Committee that his remarks covered procedures for handling mergers in general and did not necessarily reflect the views of the board's three members.

They are to be asked soon to judge the future of Conrail, the big Philadelphia-based freight line that is the subject of bidding by CSX Corp, of Richmond, Virginia, and Norfolk Southern Corp, of Norfolk, Virginia.
The board recently issued a tentative timetable for its deliberations that indicate it might not be until early 1998 before it issued a final ruling.
The board can approve a merger, reject it or amend it.

Konschnik said the board's decision on the merger would include a consideration of its impact on rail transportation in the region served and nationwide, the total charges that result from the merger, and the impact on rail workers.

Discussing the bids, up to $10 billion so far for Conrail, he said the board would also weigh the price paid: if it was so low to adequately compensate shareholders, some of whom may be Conrail workers, or so high it could damage the emerging carrier financially.

Several members, including chairman Bud Shuster (R-Penn.) and Elijah Cummings (D-Md.), both with big railroad interests in their districts, expressed concerns about the economic impact of the merger in their states.

Asked if a merger approval could be undone if the merged line did not live up to commitments made during the merger hearings on keeping lines or maintenance yards open, Konschnik said, "I couldn't rule that out."
But he added that "it would be difficult. It's an extreme remedy." He said a better tact would be to impose new conditions on the merged line, or to threaten new conditions.
Some Congressional observers said they thought such a merger "egg," once scrambled, could not be unscrambled, and any talk of such action served only as a threat.
Glenn Scammel, the majority counsel of the panel's railroad subcommittee, said he did not think that laws passed by Congress when it created Conrail would impede a merger.
The 1976 law to form Conrail out of several bankrupt eastern carriers, covered trade unions, compensation of Conrail's board of directors and the location of its headquarters, to be in Philadelphia.

Asked if action by the Surface Transportation Board, which the committee created to replace the old Interstate Commerce Commission, could displace the special Conrail laws, he said, "that's my understanding."
Committee officials said that if disputes arose over the special laws, Congress could amend them later or they could be taken up in court.
